title: The Weirdest Money in History

beats.say: October 16, 1834, London. The Houses of Parliament, the heart of Britain's government, are on fire.
Huge crowds gather along the river Thames to watch it burn.
So what started it? Not a bomb. Not lightning. Old money records.
Two cartloads of wooden sticks with notches cut into them, burned in the furnaces under the House of Lords.
Boss, these sticks barely fit in the furnace.
Then push harder. It's only wood. What could go wrong?
Those sticks had kept track of England's money for about seven hundred years.
And honestly? They're not even the weirdest money in history. Today: stones, knives, playing cards, furs and cigarettes.
First, a quick question. What actually is money?
Money is anything people agree to swap for stuff. A baker takes it because she knows the butcher will take it too.
To work well, money has to be hard to fake, not too common, and easy to pass around. But above all, people have to trust it.

show.label: What makes money work
show.sub: plus: hard to fake, hard to get, easy to pass around

beats.say: Keep that word in mind: trust. Every weird money in this video lives or dies by it.
Our first stop is ancient China, around 400 BC. China is split into rival kingdoms that fight all the time.
In kingdoms like Qi, on the east coast, people paid with bronze coins shaped like little knives.
Historians think the shape came from a real bronze tool, a small knife with a ring on the handle.
But these coins were never used as knives. They were money, with writing cast into the bronze.
One chicken, please.
That'll be one knife.
Is that a price or a threat?
Then, in 221 BC, the Qin kingdom conquered all the others. Its ruler became China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.
He made everyone use the same round coins, with a square hole in the middle. Round coins don't poke holes in your pocket.
Lesson one: money can be almost any shape, as long as everyone agrees it counts.
Now head north, to medieval Russia, and the rich trading city of Novgorod.
Winters here are brutal, and the forests are full of animals with thick, warm fur.
Furs were so valuable that pelts, the skins of animals like the marten, a small forest weasel, were used as money.
Historians still argue about how often real pelts changed hands. But the word for marten, kuna, became a word for money.
This sword costs twenty martens.
Do you take squirrels? I'm a bit short this week.
The problem? Fur wears out, and moths eat it. Imagine a bug munching through your savings.
Over time, bars of silver and then silver coins took over. But the name stuck. Croatia's money was called the kuna until 2023.
Meanwhile in England, the king's money office, called the Exchequer, had to record who had paid their taxes.
Most people couldn't read, but anyone can count notches. So the clerks used wooden sticks called tallies.
A clerk cut notches into the stick. A notch as wide as your palm meant a thousand pounds.
Then he split the stick down its length. Both halves carried the same notches.
The taxpayer kept the longer half, called the stock. The Exchequer kept the shorter half, called the foil.
To check a payment, you pushed the halves back together. If the notches and the wood lined up, the record was real.
Try faking that. You'd need the other half, and no two sticks split the same way.
England kept using tallies for centuries, until 1826. Which brings us back to 1834, and the pile of old sticks nobody wanted.
Burning them in furnaces under the House of Lords overheated the chimneys. By the next morning, most of the old palace was gone.
The famous writer Charles Dickens later mocked the whole mess in a speech.
The stove, overgorged with these preposterous sticks, set fire to the panelling; the panelling set fire to the House of Lords; the House of Lords set fire to the House of Commons.

show.text: The stove, overgorged with these preposterous sticks, set fire to the panelling; the panelling set fire to the House of Lords; the House of Lords set fire to the House of Commons.
show.who: Charles Dickens, speech in London, 27 June 1855

beats.say: The new palace built after the fire is the one you know today, with the clock tower holding Big Ben.
Next, Sweden in the 1600s. It owned one of the biggest copper mines in the world, at Falun.
So Sweden made money out of copper. One catch: copper is much cheaper than silver.
The coin was worth what its metal was worth. So a copper coin worth ten silver dalers had to be a giant slab of copper.
In 1644 Sweden made exactly that: a flat plate that weighed almost twenty kilos.

show.label: Swedish 10-daler copper plate, 1644
show.sub: about the weight of a six-year-old child

beats.say: I'd like to buy a cow, please.
Lovely. Did you bring a cart for the money?
So in 1661, when a bank in Stockholm called Stockholms Banco started printing Europe's first banknotes, people loved them.
A note was a promise: bring this paper to the bank, and get your copper. Way lighter to carry.
But the bank lent out far more notes than it had copper to back them.
When people rushed to swap paper for copper, the bank couldn't pay. It soon collapsed, and Palmstruch ended up in prison.
Lesson: paper money only works if people trust the promise behind it.
Now cross the Atlantic to 1685, and New France, the French colony in what is now Canada.
Its money manager was an official called the intendant, Jacques de Meulles. He had soldiers to pay, and almost no coins.
The ship bringing money from France was late. And the soldiers were getting impatient.
Sir, where's our pay?
Funny you should ask. Do you like card games?
De Meulles took ordinary playing cards, wrote amounts on them, signed them and added his seal.
He promised to swap every card for real coins when the ship arrived. So the cards worked, because people trusted him.
Did I just get paid with a playing card?
Yes. Please don't play poker with your wages.
And when the ship finally came, he kept his word and paid out real coins.
The king back in France didn't like it. Cards were easy to fake, he worried. Anyone with a pen could try to make their own money.
Still, the colony used card money on and off for decades. After Britain took Canada, France paid back only a quarter of the cards' value, and by 1771 even that was worthless.
Now the most famous weird money of all. Yap, a group of small islands in the Pacific Ocean.
For centuries its people used giant stone discs with a hole in the middle, called rai, as a kind of money.
The biggest known one is about three point six metres wide and weighs about four tonnes. That's heavier than two cars.

show.label: Biggest known rai stone, Yap
show.sub: about 4 tonnes, heavier than two cars

beats.say: The stone came from Palau, islands over four hundred kilometres away. Men cut it, then brought it home by canoe or raft across open sea.
Some died on the way. That's what made rai valuable: it was really, really hard to get.
And here's the weird part. Big rai usually didn't move. When one changed owners, everybody simply agreed and remembered who owned it now.
That stone is yours now.
Wonderful. I'll leave it right where it is.
An American anthropologist, William Henry Furness, visited in 1903 and wrote about one family that was rich because of a stone on the sea floor.
Long ago, a storm forced the crew to cut the stone loose from its raft. It sank. But everyone agreed it still counted.
The purchasing power of that stone remains, therefore, as valid as if it were leaning visibly against the side of the owner's house.

show.text: The purchasing power of that stone remains, therefore, as valid as if it were leaning visibly against the side of the owner's house.
show.who: William Henry Furness III, The Island of Stone Money (1910)

beats.say: Then came David O'Keefe, an Irish-American captain shipwrecked near Yap in 1871. He brought rai from Palau in bulk on his ship, cut with iron tools.
He traded them for dried coconut and sea cucumbers. But Yapese people valued his easy stones less than the old, hard-won ones.
More money, less effort, less value. That's the idea behind inflation, island style.
Our last stop is more serious. During World War Two, millions of soldiers were held as prisoners of war.
One of them was Richard Radford, a young British soldier who had studied economics. He was captured in Libya in 1942.
He was held in camps in Italy, then in Bavaria, in Germany. Life there was hard. Food was short, and nobody knew when the war would end.
Prisoners got parcels from the Red Cross, a charity that helps people in wars. Inside: jam, chocolate, sugar, and cigarettes.
Everyone traded. And soon one item became the money: the cigarette. Even non-smokers took them, because they knew others would.
Cheese for seven!
Seven cigarettes? I'll give you six and a compliment.
Prices were posted on notice boards. Radford noted that a shirt cost around eighty cigarettes.

show.label: Prison camp price, as recorded by Radford
show.sub: for one shirt (60 to 120, depending on quality)

beats.say: And the camp even had inflation. When a big delivery of cigarettes arrived, there was suddenly lots of money, so prices shot up.
Then people smoked their money. Cigarettes got scarce again, and prices fell.
Some prisoners even rolled thinner cigarettes from the same tobacco, the way crooks once shaved metal off coins.
Radford survived the war and published all of this in 1945. Economists still read his paper today.
So stones, sticks, knives, furs, cards and cigarettes. None of it is worth much on its own.
Money works because we all agree that it works. Your banknotes and your banking app run on the same thing as a stone at the bottom of the sea: trust.

description:
Giant stones that never moved, bronze coins shaped like knives, playing cards signed as cash, notched sticks that burned down Parliament, a 20-kilo copper coin and cigarettes in a WWII prison camp. We tour history's weirdest money and use it to explain, in plain words, what makes money work: trust, scarcity, inflation and counterfeiting.
